content: Nigella damascena, commonly known as Love-in-a-mist, is an annual flowering plant that belongs to the buttercup family, Ranunculaceae. It is native to southern Europe, though it has spread to more northern parts of Europe, as well as North Africa and southwest Asia. Additionally, it is frequently cultivated in gardens across North America. The plant is often found in neglected, damp areas of land. The common name Love-in-a-mist is derived from the appearance of the flower, which is surrounded by a ring of finely divided, lace-like bracts. It is also sometimes referred to as Devil in the Bush. The plant typically grows to a height of 20–50 cm and features pinnately divided, thread-like, alternate leaves. The flowers of Nigella damascena come in shades of white, pink, pale blue, or pale purple and have 5–10 sepals. The true petals are small, clawed structures located at the base of the stamens. Notably, the sepals are the only colored part of the perianth. The compound pistil consists of 4–5 carpels, each with an erect style. The flowers bloom during May and June. The fruit of the plant is a large, inflated capsule that develops from a compound ovary. This capsule is composed of several united follicles, each containing numerous seeds. This type of fruit structure is unusual for members of the buttercup family. By late summer, the capsule turns brown and is often used in dried flower arrangements. Several cultivars of Nigella damascena are available, offering flowers in various shades of pink and purple. Popular cultivars include 'Albion,' 'Blue Midget,' 'Cambridge Blue,' 'Miss Jekyll,' 'Mulberry Rose,' 'Oxford Blue,' and 'Persian Jewels.' It is important to note that a related species, Nigella sativa, and not Nigella damascena, is the source of the spice known as nigella, kalonji, or black cumin.
